client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. Every time there's a family get-together, I just... can't enjoy it the way I used to. It's like there's this huge empty space where she used to be, and I don't know if talking about it is actually going to change how I feel.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a quiet but persistent ache — not overwhelmed in an acute way, but living with this steady awareness of her absence, especially in the moments that used to feel joyful. That kind of grief can feel almost disorienting, like the world kept moving but something fundamental shifted. I'm curious — when you're at those family gatherings and notice that empty space, what thoughts tend to go through your mind in those moments?

client: Mostly I think things like "she should be here" or "she would have loved this" — and then I feel this wave of guilt because everyone else seems to be laughing and carrying on, and I'm just standing there feeling hollow. Sometimes I even get a little resentful, which makes me feel worse, like I'm somehow ruining it for myself or being selfish. It's this spiral where I can't just let myself be sad without also judging myself for being sad.
therapist: What you're describing — grief layered with guilt layered with self-judgment — is such a painful tangle, and it makes sense that it feels exhausting rather than just sad. The resentment you feel isn't selfishness; it's actually a very human response when you're hurting and the world around you seems to be moving at a different pace than your heart is. I'd gently invite you to consider: if a close friend told you they felt exactly this way after losing someone they loved, would you tell them they were being selfish — or would you offer them some compassion?

client: I mean, obviously I wouldn't tell a friend they were being selfish — I'd probably hold their hand and tell them it makes complete sense to feel that way. But it's so much harder to apply that same logic to myself, and honestly that reframe feels a little too simple, like knowing I "should" be kinder to myself doesn't automatically make me feel it. It's like there's a gap between understanding something intellectually and actually believing it in the moment when I'm standing in my aunt's kitchen feeling like a ghost at my own family gathering.
therapist: You're naming something really important — that insight alone doesn't close the emotional gap, and it can even feel a little hollow when someone offers it as though understanding should be enough. That gap between knowing and *feeling* is real, and it's actually where a lot of the deeper work lives. I'm wondering — in that moment in your aunt's kitchen, what do you think it would take, even something small, to feel less like a ghost and more like someone who is allowed to be both grieving *and* present at the same time?

client: Honestly, the only thing I can think of is maybe if someone in my family actually talked about her — like really mentioned her name, shared a memory, instead of this unspoken agreement to just... keep things light. But I'm also scared that if I'm the one to bring her up, I'll start crying and make everyone uncomfortable, and then I'll feel guilty for shifting the mood. So I end up staying quiet and feeling even more alone, which I know doesn't help, but I don't see a way around it.
therapist: There's something really poignant about what you've just uncovered — you actually *know* what might help (hearing her name, sharing a memory), but the fear of being "too much" for others keeps you locked in silence and loneliness. It's worth gently questioning that fear though: is it possible that other family members are also quietly missing her and might actually feel *relieved* if you opened that door, rather than burdened? What do you imagine might happen if you tested that assumption — even in a small, low-stakes way with just one family member you trust?

client: Maybe my cousin Sarah — she was really close to my grandmother too, and I've caught her looking a little lost at gatherings as well. But I'm worried that even a small conversation could open up something neither of us is ready to handle, like what if we both just fall apart and it makes the whole day harder instead of better. I guess I can see the logic in what you're saying, but I'm not convinced that sharing the grief is going to feel like relief rather than just... more pain.
therapist: It's really meaningful that you've already noticed Sarah — that quiet recognition between the two of you suggests there might already be an unspoken connection around this grief, just waiting for a small opening. Your concern that sharing might mean "falling apart" is worth examining though, because it carries an assumption that falling apart together would be a bad thing — when sometimes being witnessed in your sadness by someone who loved the same person is exactly what makes grief feel less like a weight you're carrying alone. I'm curious — when you imagine that conversation with Sarah going *well*, what does that actually look like?

client: When I try to imagine it going well, I picture us maybe stepping outside together, and one of us just saying her name, and then sharing some small memory — like how she always burned the rolls at Thanksgiving but insisted they were perfect. And in that version it actually does feel like something loosens a little, like exhaling after holding your breath. But then I catch myself thinking that's probably just a fantasy, and the real version would be messier and more awkward, and I'd probably end up comforting Sarah instead of feeling any relief myself.
therapist: That image you just painted — stepping outside, saying her name, the burned rolls — that wasn't a fantasy, that was your own wisdom showing you what healing could feel like, and it's worth taking seriously. I also notice you quickly dismissed it by predicting mess and awkwardness, and that even in the "good" version you ended up taking care of Sarah rather than letting yourself be held too — which sounds like a familiar pattern of putting your own needs last. What would it mean for you to let yourself be comforted in that moment, rather than being the one who holds it together?

client: Honestly, that question makes me uncomfortable in a way I wasn't expecting, because I think letting myself be comforted would feel almost selfish — like I'm burdening Sarah with my emotions when she's grieving too. I've always been the one who keeps it together in my family, and I'm not even sure I know how to receive comfort without immediately trying to deflect it or minimize what I'm feeling. It's like I don't quite believe I'm allowed to need that from someone else.
therapist: What you just said — "I don't quite believe I'm allowed to need that from someone else" — feels like something really central, almost like a quiet rule you've been living by for a long time without fully realizing it. It's not selfish to have needs; it's human, and the fact that Sarah is grieving too doesn't mean there isn't room for both of you to give *and* receive — that's actually what real connection looks like. I'm gently curious: where do you think that belief came from, that needing comfort from others is a burden rather than something you're allowed to ask for?

client: I think it probably goes back to when I was younger — my mom had a lot on her plate and I learned pretty early that the way to be loved was to be easy, to not add to her stress. I never really thought of it as a rule I made for myself, it just became who I am, and now sitting here I feel a strange mix of recognition and resistance, like part of me is nodding and another part wants to say "that was a long time ago, it doesn't still apply." But maybe it does still apply, and that's the uncomfortable part.
therapist: That moment of simultaneous recognition and resistance you're describing is actually really significant — it means part of you is already questioning whether that old rule still serves you, even if another part is protecting it because it once kept you safe and loved. The child who learned to be "easy" was doing something incredibly adaptive given what she needed then, but you're not in that kitchen anymore, and the people in your life now — like Sarah — may be far more capable of holding your needs than your younger self had reason to believe. What might it feel like to try, even just once, to let that old rule be wrong?

client: Letting that old rule be wrong feels terrifying in a way I can't quite articulate, like if I stop being the person who holds it together, I don't know who I am instead. And there's a part of me that's worried if I let Sarah see me fall apart over my grandmother, she'll think less of me, even though logically I know that probably isn't true. I guess what I'm realizing is that the rule feels less like a choice and more like the floor I've been standing on, and you're asking me to step off it without knowing what's underneath.
therapist: The image of it being the *floor* — not just a habit but the very ground you stand on — really captures how deep this goes, and it makes complete sense that questioning it feels less like growth and more like freefall. But I want to offer you something gently: you've already started stepping off it, right here in this conversation, by saying out loud that you need comfort, that you've been lonely in your grief, that the rule might not be serving you anymore — and you haven't disappeared. What do you notice about yourself in this moment, having said all of that?

client: I notice I feel a little shaky but also... lighter isn't quite the right word, maybe just less compressed, like something that was held very tight has loosened slightly. I haven't disappeared, you're right about that, and I'm still sitting here which is more than I expected when I started talking. But I'm also aware that this feels safer here than it will feel at the next family gathering, and I'm not sure I can carry whatever this is out of this room and into real life.
therapist: That loosening you're feeling right now — even if it's small and a little shaky — is real, and it belongs to you, not to this room. What happened here today wasn't magic I created for you; it came from your own willingness to look honestly at something you've been carrying for a very long time, which means that capacity travels with you. I'm wondering — what's one tiny, concrete thing you could do before the next gathering, maybe just a text to Sarah, that would let this conversation be a small bridge rather than something that stays sealed in here?
